questions.q: How many test cases does Forge run per fuzz test function by default?
questions.explain: Forge generates 256 random test cases per fuzz function by default, configurable via [fuzz].runs in foundry.toml.

questions.q: What makes a test function a fuzz test in Foundry?
options: Giving the test function a typed parameter, which Forge fills with random values across many runs
Calling vm.fuzz() at the start of the test
questions.explain: Any typed parameter on a test function is automatically fuzzed by Forge — no special annotation or naming convention is required.

questions.q: What is the key difference between `vm.assume` and `bound()` for constraining a fuzzed input?
options: They are identical in every way
vm.assume rejects (discards) runs outside the condition; bound() clamps the value into range so every run counts
bound() only works with address types
vm.assume runs are slower than bound() runs
questions.explain: vm.assume throws away non-matching runs (too many rejections and Forge gives up), while bound() clamps the value in place, so bound() is usually preferred.

questions.q: What does setting a fixed `seed` in foundry.toml's [fuzz] table accomplish?
options: It increases the number of runs automatically
It makes a fuzzing run reproducible, which matters when debugging a specific failure
questions.explain: A fixed seed produces the same sequence of random inputs on each run, letting you reproduce and debug an exact failing case.

questions.q: What does a fuzz test still NOT cover, according to this lesson?
options: Boundary values like zero or max uint256
Sequences of calls across multiple functions and multiple actors
questions.explain: A fuzz test calls one function, once, per run — it doesn't test multi-call sequences across functions and actors, which is what invariant testing (Lesson 3) adds.
